content: Individuals were given the freedom to decline participation in data collection activities without any obligation to provide reasons for their decision. Prior to the participatory action research (PAR) sessions, individual in-depth interviews (IDIs) and focus group discussions (FGDs) were conducted. These interviews and discussions were guided by a structured 42-item interview guide, which was developed based on findings from previous research on values and preferences. The guide was translated into local languages by implementing institutions and piloted by local teams before use. During interviews, all questions were asked in a consistent order, but interviewers introduced additional context-specific probes when further elaboration was needed. In most sessions, interviewers were accompanied by note-takers, and gender-matching between interviewers and participants was implemented when necessary. However, in certain cases, such as interviews with men who have sex with men (MSM) using drugs in the Philippines, the interviewer conducted the session alone. Participants provided basic socio-demographic information, including age, gender identity, area of residence, and education level. Additional details, such as ethnicity, hepatitis C virus (HCV) status, or engagement in sex work, were only recorded if voluntarily disclosed. COVID-19 prevention measures influenced the number of participants in group discussions, with most groups consisting of five to seven participants. Audio recordings were made for most interviews and discussions, and these recordings were transcribed into a question-by-question matrix in Microsoft Excel®. Transcripts were prepared in local languages, and their accuracy was verified against the recordings by lead on-site consultants. Any errors identified were promptly corrected. Recordings were deleted after the analysis phase was completed. In cases where participants declined to consent to audio recording, interviewers directly typed responses into the Excel matrix. All participants were offered the opportunity to review their transcripts, and in some cases, such as in Ukraine, transcripts were returned to participants for comments. The PAR sessions employed community-based research approaches that emphasized participation, decision-making, critical thinking, and information sharing. These sessions were conducted in all countries and with all population groups except healthcare workers (HCWs). Sub-groups engaged in four exercises: roles and responsibilities, mapping, decision-making, and prioritization. These exercises explored participants' perceptions of their societal roles, access to resources, and risks related to HCV infection. Participants also discussed how HCV testing services could be proposed, including locations, timing, and personnel involved. They considered institutional and healthcare system adjustments needed to address community needs, barriers to HCV care, and inequalities in access to testing services. Data collection, transcription, and analysis occurred concurrently. Each implementing institution had access only to its own participants' data, which was shared with FIND and the University of Zaragoza. A thematic approach was used to analyze findings, filtering by participants' sex, education, and area of residence. Findings from IDIs and FGDs were compared with results from PAR sessions. Field notes and reflexive memos taken during data encounters were also considered. Each institution produced a country-specific report summarizing major findings, which were subsequently coded to identify deviant cases and detect similarities and discrepancies in responses regarding HCV self-testing (HCVST) delivery models. Ethical considerations were strictly adhered to, including compliance with national norms for formative research and data protection. Participants provided written or verbal informed consent and were informed about the study's goals, potential risks, and their rights, including the right to withdraw at any time. Measures were implemented to protect participants' privacy and confidentiality, such as anonymizing data and deleting recordings after analysis. No personal identifiers were transcribed, and socio-demographic data were collected only with participants' consent. A total of 920 participants were recruited, including MSM, people living with HIV (PLHIV), people who inject drugs (PWID), transgender individuals, HCWs, and members of the general population (GP). Participants were distributed across WHO regions, with varying levels of urban residency and education. Data collection methods included IDIs, FGDs, and PAR sessions, with some participants involved in multiple activities. Participants reflected on the perceived benefits and disadvantages of HCVST. Transgender participants, for example, viewed HCVST as an innovative tool that could increase testing and treatment demand while offering privacy and convenience. However, they also highlighted challenges such as difficulties in interpreting results, the need for preand post-test counseling, and barriers related to literacy, stigma, and access to healthcare. Concerns about social harm, such as depression or loss of relationships, were also noted. Participants emphasized the importance of addressing these challenges through awareness campaigns, anti-stigma measures, and supportive healthcare services.
